title: The patient who declines radiographs before an extraction
stem:
A 41-year-old office manager attends with a broken-down, tender **lower left second molar**. After discussion she wants the tooth extracted rather than restored.

When you explain you need a radiograph before extracting it, she declines: *"I don't want any X-rays — I've read they cause cancer, and I had a scan at the hospital last year anyway. Can't you just take the tooth out?"*

She is otherwise fit and well, is not pregnant, communicates clearly, and understands she is choosing between restoring and removing the tooth. Clinically the tooth is a heavily broken-down lower second molar with lingual caries extending subgingivally; you cannot assess root morphology, curvature, or the relationship to the inferior dental canal without imaging.

domains.name: Information gathering, assimilation & diagnosis
domains.model_answer:
My headline: this is a **consent and communication scenario dressed up as an extraction** — the clinical dentistry is straightforward, and the task is to explore her concern, give her the information she actually needs, and reach a shared decision she can validly consent to.

**First, explore, don't contradict.** I would ask open questions, because I can't address a concern I haven't understood: what has she read, and where? What was the hospital scan — a CT carries hundreds of times the dose of a dental periapical, and if she's conflating the two, that's the crux. Has she had a bad experience? Is there any chance of pregnancy, because that's a separate justification conversation and she may be silently worrying about it.

**Capacity check, done quietly in my head:** under the **Mental Capacity Act 2005** I assume capacity unless there's reason to doubt it. She understands the information, retains it, weighs it — she's weighing it right now, just with inaccurate inputs — and communicates a clear decision. She has capacity. A decision I disagree with is not evidence of incapacity; that's principle 3 of the Act, an unwise decision is not an incapacitous one.

**Clinical information gathering** carries on in parallel: pain history and pulpal diagnosis for the lower left seven; charting and periodontal status; and specifically what I can and cannot determine without imaging — I can diagnose the tooth as unrestorable clinically, but I cannot assess root number, curvature, ankylosis, or **proximity to the inferior dental canal**, and for a lower second molar that last one is a *Montgomery*-material fact.

**The knowledge I need at my fingertips, because the examiner will probe it:** a periapical radiograph is roughly 0.005 mSv — of the order of **less than a day of UK natural background radiation**, and comparable to a couple of hours on a flight. Under **IRMER 2017** I'm only proposing it because it's justified: the benefit (safe extraction planning, avoiding nerve injury and surprise surgical complications) outweighs that tiny risk. FGDP/CGDent *Selection Criteria for Dental Radiography* supports pre-extraction imaging of a broken-down molar precisely because it changes technique and consent.

domains.name: Management of scenario
domains.model_answer:
Today's management is a **conversation, not a procedure** — and I would be explicit that I'm in no rush to pick up forceps.

**Step one: validate, then inform.** "You're right that X-rays use ionising radiation, and it's sensible to question that." Then give honest scale, because respect for her autonomy means giving her real numbers, not reassurance-noises: a small dental X-ray is a fraction of a single day's natural background radiation; the hospital scan she had was a much bigger dose, and this doesn't meaningfully add to it. I'd use a comparison she can hold onto — "about the same as a short flight".

**Step two: explain why this radiograph, this time, changes what I do** — because IRMER justification is patient-specific, and so is persuasion: her tooth is a lower second molar sitting near the nerve that supplies feeling to her lip and chin. Without the image I don't know how curved or bulbous the roots are or how close the canal runs, so I can't warn her properly about nerve injury, can't plan whether this is a simple or surgical extraction, and I'm more likely to have a complication mid-procedure that turns a ten-minute extraction into a referral.

**Step three: lay out the options honestly, including the ones I don't recommend:** (1) radiograph then extraction — my recommendation; (2) extraction without imaging — I would explain that I'm not willing to do this, because I can't obtain valid consent for risks I can't assess, and proceeding blind falls below the standard of care; (3) delay — go away, read the information sheet I give her, decide later, with analgesia and clear advice in the meantime; (4) do nothing at all — with the honest risks: pain, infection, and the possibility of presenting later as an emergency.

**Red flags and urgency:** there's no swelling, no systemic upset, no red flags — so there is genuinely time for her to think, and saying that out loud lowers the temperature of the whole conversation.

In my experience of how this actually goes: once the hospital-CT confusion is untangled and the dose is put in context, most patients consent. The scenario is testing whether I educate and respect, or capitulate and drill — or worse, extract blind.

domains.name: Management planning & execution
domains.model_answer:
**If she consents to the radiograph (most likely outcome):** I take a periapical of the lower left seven using rectangular collimation and optimal technique, because IRMER's optimisation duty means every exposure is as low as reasonably practicable — that's a nice thing to say out loud, because it shows her concern and my legal duty point the same way. Then normal planning: assess roots and canal proximity, consent for extraction including the specific *Montgomery*-material risks for this tooth (pain, bleeding, dry socket, root fracture, **temporary or permanent altered sensation of lip/chin/tongue** with my best estimate of likelihood given the anatomy, oro-antral issues not relevant this far posterior), then extract, with post-op instructions written and verbal.

**If she maintains refusal of imaging:** I don't extract blind, and I don't abandon her either. My plan: manage today's symptoms — caries excavation and a dressing if pulpal, or analgesia advice per SDCEP *Management of Acute Dental Problems*; ibuprofen and/or paracetamol at standard doses [verify against current BNF/SDCEP]; no antibiotics, because there's no spreading infection or systemic involvement and SDCEP is clear they're not indicated for localised pulpitis. Give her written information on dental radiation doses, offer a review appointment rather than a doorstep decision, and offer a second opinion — including that another dentist is entitled to take the same view I do. If she ever develops swelling or systemic symptoms, the urgency calculus changes and we revisit.

**Sequencing matters and I'd name it:** stabilise (symptom control today) → definitive (imaging plus extraction when she's ready) → maintenance (prevent the next broken-down molar: caries risk assessment, diet, fluoride per *Delivering Better Oral Health*, sensible recall per NICE guidance).

**Execution safeguards:** if the radiograph shows intimate canal involvement or unfavourable roots, my own referral threshold applies — I would refer to oral surgery rather than have my pride make this complicated, and I'd tell her that's a possibility in advance so a referral doesn't feel like a failure.

domains.name: Professionalism, ethics & medicolegal
domains.model_answer:
**The ethical spine of this case:** her autonomy is real and so is my professional integrity — respecting a refusal does not oblige me to provide substandard treatment. She is entitled to decline the radiograph; she is not entitled to an extraction performed below the standard of care, and I'm entitled — obliged, actually — to decline to provide that, while making sure she isn't left without care. That's the balance of GDC *Standards* principle 1 (patients' interests first) with principle 7 (work within your knowledge and skills, provide good quality care based on current evidence).

**Consent as a process:** *Montgomery* requires me to share the material risks and reasonable alternatives — and here the honest disclosure includes a slightly unusual one: "without the X-ray, I cannot tell you how likely nerve injury is, and that itself is why I won't proceed." Consent she gives for a blind extraction wouldn't be valid, because neither of us knows what she'd be consenting to. I'd also document that radiation risk was discussed with actual figures.

**Documentation, in detail because this is the medicolegal heart of it:** her exact concern in her own words where possible; the information given, including dose comparisons; the options offered including doing nothing; what she decided; that capacity was assessed and present; the written information provided; and the safety-netting given. If she later suffers harm — an emergency presentation, or an extraction elsewhere that damages her nerve — my notes are the evidence that she made an informed choice and I made a professional one.

**Safety-netting, out loud and written down:** "If you get swelling of your face, difficulty swallowing, fever, or pain that stops you sleeping, contact us the same day — don't wait for your next appointment. Out of hours, call NHS 111." Refusal scenarios need *stronger* safety-netting than normal ones, because the untreated disease is still in her mouth.

**Door stays open, ego stays out:** I'd close with something like "whatever you decide, you're welcome back and we'll take it from there" — because the worst medicolegal and human outcome is a patient who felt lectured, disappeared, and came back as an emergency. And beyond this — if she raised something like a needle-phobia-level radiographic anxiety — I'd seek advice, because escalating to senior or specialist input when a consent situation exceeds my experience scores up, not down.

marks_lost: Extracting without imaging "because the patient insisted" — patient choice does not validate substandard care.
Dismissing her concern ("X-rays are perfectly safe") instead of exploring where it came from and giving real numbers.
Failing to mention the inferior dental nerve as the specific reason imaging matters for this tooth.
Confusing refusal of a radiograph with lack of capacity — an unwise decision is not an incapacitous one (MCA 2005, principle 3).
No fallback plan for maintained refusal — symptom control, written information, review, second opinion.
Prescribing antibiotics for localised pulpitis to "buy time".
Thin documentation — this case is won or lost in the notes.
No safety-netting for the untreated tooth.

probes.q: Give the patient an actual sense of the dose of a periapical radiograph.
probes.a: Around 0.005 millisieverts — less than a single day of UK natural background radiation (about 2.7 mSv per year), and similar to the cosmic-ray dose from an hour or two of flying. A hospital CT of the abdomen, by comparison, is on the order of a thousand periapicals. Figures like these, offered without condescension, are usually what actually changes the conversation.

probes.q: She asks: "If I sign a form saying it's my own risk, will you take it out without the X-ray?"
probes.a: No — and I'd explain why kindly: a signature can't make consent valid when neither of us knows the risks, because I can't quantify the chance of nerve injury or a fractured root without the image. A disclaimer doesn't transfer my professional responsibility to her; the GDC and the courts judge me by the standard of care, not by the paperwork. What I can offer is time, information, and alternatives.

probes.q: What are the three IRMER 2017 duty-holder roles relevant here, and who holds them in practice?
probes.a: Referrer (supplies clinical information justifying the request), practitioner (justifies the exposure — decides benefit outweighs risk), and operator (carries out the exposure and the practical optimisation). In general dental practice the dentist commonly acts as referrer and practitioner and may also be the operator; the employer holds separate duties as the legal person, including procedures, training and dose reference levels.

probes.q: How would this scenario change if she were 15 rather than 41?
probes.a: Capacity becomes Gillick competence: can she understand, weigh and communicate this specific decision? If she's Gillick-competent she can consent to the radiograph and extraction, though good practice involves parents where she agrees. Radiation justification is also stricter — children's tissues are more radiosensitive, so the optimisation duty bites harder. And a refusal of clearly beneficial treatment in a minor raises the question of parental consent and, in extremes, best-interests processes — though for an elective extraction the realistic answer is time and rapport, not compulsion.

references: GDC Standards for the Dental Team — principles 1, 2, 3 and 7
IRMER 2017 — justification and optimisation; duty-holder roles
FGDP/CGDent — Selection Criteria for Dental Radiography
SDCEP — Management of Acute Dental Problems
